subject: NA's in x. What to do?

messages.author: 81ff9f426c4adffa
messages.subject: NA's in x. What to do?
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm really just getting started with Stan and learning as I go here. I have a dataset (attached) of primates and I'm trying to do a multinomial logistic regression. I hijacked the basic code from another user who posted here, and tried to modify it for the purposes of monkeys! The basic idea is that these species are classified based on how endangered they are (from 0 to 4) by a conservation organization. These values are ordinal integers (so categorical classification). I have data about each species (things like it's geographic range size, average precipitation where it lives, body mass, etc) and I'm trying to see which of these variables may be associated (perhaps causing) any given species' risk of extinction. 

The problem is that for each of these variables, I have NA's for some of the variables for some species (for example, one species the body mass might not be known and for another the range size is unknown). There are 108 species in this test dataset, so I have a lot of wiggle room, but if I removed any variable that had any NA's, I would pretty much remove them all. 

When I run the model in rstan, I get the following:

TRANSLATING MODEL 'mnl_code' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'mnl_code' NOW.
Error in FUN(c("K", "N", "D", "y", "x")[[5L]], ...) : 
  Stan does not support NA (in x) in data
failed to preprocess the data; sampling not done

While I know that NA's are a pain, it seems like there should be a simple workaround for this. Doing some digging through the stan-reference, I can't seem to find a way to address this. Any support would be great.

Here is my code (and the dataset it attached for your pleasure):


##
## Fit with Stan
##

monkey_code <-  '
data {
int<lower=2> K;
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1> D;
int<lower=0,upper=K> y[N];
vector[D] x[N];
}
parameters {
matrix[K,D] beta;
}
model {
for (k in 1:K)
for (d in 1:D)
beta[k,d] ~ normal(0,5);
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta * x[n]));
}
'

## Set up data for Stan
x <- cbind(1, 
           prim1$X28.1_Precip_Mean_mm, prim1$latrange, prim1$X5.1_AdultBodyMass_g, 
          prim1$X26.1_GR_Area_km2)
y <- as.numeric(prim$risknum)

prim_data <- list(K = 4,
                  N = 108,
                  D = 5,
                  y = y,
                  x = x
)
## K = number of outcome possibilities  
# N = number of rows of data
# D = Number of predictor variables
# y = random variable
# x = cb of all predictors 

fit <- stan(model_code = monkey_code, data = prim_data, 
            iter = 1000, chains = 1)

On Friday, May 31, 2013 5:08:52 PM UTC-4, Kevin Bracy Knight wrote:
I'm really just getting started with Stan and learning as I go here. I have a dataset (attached) of primates and I'm trying to do a multinomial logistic regression. I hijacked the basic code from another user who posted here, and tried to modify it for the purposes of monkeys! The basic idea is that these species are classified based on how endangered they are (from 0 to 4) by a conservation organization. These values are ordinal integers (so categorical classification).

I believe you would want to use an ordered logistic model (section 11.6 of the manual) rather than multinomial logistic model (section 11.5). But the problem of missingness remains. There is some stuff in section 8.1 of the manual, but it is currently pretty difficult to do something good in Stan when there are arbitrary missing data patterns. And it is even more difficult when some of the missing values are discrete.

I would suggest first doing multiple imputation to create m datasets, call stan() once on each of the m datasets, and combine the results using the sflist2stanfit() function in the RStan package.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NA's in x. What to do?
parts:
The model you're starting with doesn't actually provide
a model of the predictors in x that are missing. For any
kind of full Bayesian analysis, that's where you'd need
to start. So you'd need a full joint model.

https://stat.duke.edu/node/14480

Unfortunately, as Ben pointed out, even if you had a model,
the missingness patterns you have appear to be difficult.

Andrew Gelman and Jennifer Hill have an approach to multiple imputation
which is implemented in the mi system in R:

http://www.stat.ucla.edu/~yajima/Publication/mipaper.rev04.pdf

I believe Ben's taken over the code from Yu-sung Su.

- Bob
